pr_title: Update RegionInfo data and Fix RegionInfo.CurrentRegion on Windows
pr_body:
Fixes #32753

Currently when running on Windows, the call of RegionInfo.CurrentRegion will return the region object matching CurrentCulture. Windows has different settings for the default region than the current culture. The good example is mentioned in the scenario in the attached issue which having current culture was set to `English (Europ)` and Country was set to `Netherland` and when getting CurrentRegion we return `159` because Europ doesn't have country code (because it is not a country). We suppose to return the region for `Netherland`. 
The change here is fixing this issue and updating the region data table too to reflect latest list of regions we have in the world.

issue_context.title: Region.TwoLetterISORegionName can return three numerical digits
comments:
When choosing `English (Europe)`, Windows will set the default locale to `en-150` and that will return the region's name `Europ` and TwoLetterISORegionName `150` which is correct. if you want to get the Netherlands region, you'll need to choose one of the locales:

```
English (Netherlands)
Western Frisian (Netherlands)
Low German (Netherlands)
Dutch (Netherlands)
```

Those will return `NL` as TwoLetterISORegionName.

For WinRT case, WinRT works differently as the UWP apps can have a list of default languages which is a mix from the user profile languages and app languages too. Note that  `Windows.Globalization.GeographicRegion().CodeTwoLetter` is a Windows API and not .NET API. This is by design for .NET as RegionInfo.CurrentRegion always returns the match of your Regional format setting which is the case here.

@tarekgh I don't consider an API that returns **3 digits** from a property named **TwoLetter**ISORegionName to be correct behavior. Is this documented as errata somewhere? Does the ISO define what `150` means?

From my reading, `150` seems to correspond with all custom cultures on Windows and isn't tied to Europe, so how do .NET users retrieve the region correctly?

@tarekgh In Windows 10, the user selected a "country" of `Netherlands` and "regional format" of `English (Europe)`. So how do you recommend .NET users retrieve the selected country if `RegionInfo.CurrentRegion` isn't correct?

Also, can we agree returning 3 digits from a property that is expected to return 2 letters is a bug, at least in its design?

> In Windows 10, the user selected a "country" of Netherlands and "regional format" of English (Europe)

.NET code is written before Windows 10 introduces such settings. I'll follow up with the Windows team to see if we can leverage it. But if anyone tries to create a region for en-150, they will still get `150` as the code if this is Windows/ICU behavior.

> Also, can we agree returning 3 digits from a property that is expected to return 2 letters is a bug, at least in its design?

Well, although I agree with you in principle, my agreement wouldn't change anything here as we are getting this from Windows. So, this is the decision taken by the Windows team (and properly by the standard guys as I am seeing ICU is doing the same).

review_comments:
nit, I don't think there is any value in passing in a prime number - the dictionary internally rounds up to the next prime number from its list. it's harmless though of course.

Ideally the C# compiler would know that there's N entries coming in the initializer and pass in N to the constructor.
I'll keep it as it is harmless and I am not sure what the C# initializer how it behaves there.
fine, fyi the initializer always uses the parameterless constructor, so it is a valid microoptmization to pass a size here.
So sometimes it's null terminated and sometimes not? Why does it not return ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER when it has no room to null terminate?

The doc is not ensuring returning null that is why I have to check to know if we got the null or not. 
We are requesting the 2-letters country code and I am providing a buffer of length 10 which is far enough to ensure not running into the ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER case even with null.
I would be more conservative checking null as the doc didn't ensure that and I am not sure what happen if we run on a different version of Windows.
